claim: Pigment cells in the purple sea urchin Strongylocentrotus purpuratus embryo segregate into two distinct populations: a mitotic cluster and a post-mitotic cluster.
source: We took advantage of single cell RNA-seq (scRNAseq) technology and discovered that pigment cells in the embryo segregated into two distinct populations, a mitotic cluster and a post-mitotic cluster.
evidence: The abstract directly states this finding based on scRNAseq data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Gcm is essential for expression of several genes important for pigment function.
source: Gcm is essential for expression of several genes important for pigment function, but is only transiently expressed in these cells.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data throughout the manuscript including morpholino knockdown experiments.

claim: Gcm is only transiently expressed in pigment cells.
source: Gcm is essential for expression of several genes important for pigment function, but is only transiently expressed in these cells.
evidence: The abstract states this and it is supported by single-cell RNA-seq data showing dynamic gcm expression across developmental stages.

claim: New members of the fmo family are expressed selectively in pigment cells of the embryonic and in the coelomic cells of the adult.
source: These genes include new members of the fmo family that are expressed selectively in pigment cells of the embryonic and in the coelomic cells of the adult - both cell-types having immune functions.
evidence: The abstract states this finding, which is supported by qPCR and in situ hybridization data in the results section.

claim: Both embryonic pigment cells and adult coelomic cells have immune functions.
source: These genes include new members of the fmo family that are expressed selectively in pigment cells of the embryonic and in the coelomic cells of the adult - both cell-types having immune functions.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by citations to previous work on immune functions of these cells.

claim: Pigmentation in individuals or species can change annually or instantaneously for camouflage.
source: Pigmentation in an individual or in a species can change annually, or even instantaneously for camouflage for exmple arctic hares or cephalopod mollusks and chameleons respectively, making pigmentation even more dynamic in response to the environment.
evidence: This is stated as general knowledge with examples provided (arctic hares, cephalopods, chameleons).

claim: The adult purple sea urchin is intensely dark purple due to a family of polyketides, including echinochrome and various related spinochromes.
source: The adult of this echinoderm is intensely dark purple as a result of a family of polyketides, including echinochrome and various related spinochromes (Anderson et al., 1969).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a citation to Anderson et al., 1969.

claim: S. purpuratus larvae are pigmented due to the accumulation of a red/orange pigment in single cells embedded in and scattered throughout the aboral ectodermal layer.
source: Furthermore, like most sea urchins, S. purpuratus larvae are pigmented due to the accumulation of a red/orange pigment in single cells embedded in, and scattered throughout, the aboral ectodermal layer (Gibson and Burke, 1985; Griffiths, 1965; Gustafson and Wolpert, 1967; Kominami et al., 2001; McClendon, 1912).
evidence: This is stated with multiple citations to previous work.

claim: The larval pigment is a napthoquinone called echinochrome A.
source: This pigment is a napthoquinone called echinochrome A, which accumulates in the pigment cell precursors during gastrulation in S. purpuratus (Calestani et al., 2003; Griffiths, 1965; Kuhn and Wallenfels, 1940; Oulhen and Wessel, 2016).
evidence: This is stated with citations to previous work identifying the pigment.

claim: Echinochrome A accumulates in the pigment cell precursors during gastrulation in S. purpuratus.
source: This pigment is a napthoquinone called echinochrome A, which accumulates in the pigment cell precursors during gastrulation in S. purpuratus (Calestani et al., 2003; Griffiths, 1965; Kuhn and Wallenfels, 1940; Oulhen and Wessel, 2016).
evidence: This is stated with citations to previous work.

claim: Mutations that affect the pigmentation pathway lead to albinism.
source: Mutations that affect the pigmentation pathway lead to albinism (Calestani et al., 2003; Oulhen and Wessel, 2016; Wessel et al., 2020), and adult sea urchins that lack pigments are less resistant to environmental challenges (Wessel et al., 2020).
evidence: This is stated with citations to previous work.

claim: Adult sea urchins that lack pigments are less resistant to environmental challenges.
source: Mutations that affect the pigmentation pathway lead to albinism (Calestani et al., 2003; Oulhen and Wessel, 2016; Wessel et al., 2020), and adult sea urchins that lack pigments are less resistant to environmental challenges (Wessel et al., 2020).
evidence: This is stated with a citation to Wessel et al., 2020.

claim: Sea urchin larval pigment cells have an essential role in the innate immune defense system.
source: A known function of sea urchin larval pigment cells includes an essential role in the innate immune defense system (Buckley and Rast, 2017; Ch Ho et al., 2016; Hibino et al., 2006; Hira et al., 2020; Kiselev et al., 2013; Ransick and Davidson, 2006; Schrankel et al., 2016; Solek et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated with multiple citations to previous work.

claim: When larvae are exposed to bacteria, pigment cells migrate from the ectoderm to the gut and interact with other immune cells.
source: When larvae are exposed to bacteria, pigment cells migrate from the ectoderm to the gut, a site for invading microbes, and interact with other immune cells (Ch Ho et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated with a citation to Ch Ho et al., 2016.

claim: Pigment cell-cell interaction is at least in part regulated by IL17 cytokine.
source: This cell-cell interaction is at least in part regulated by IL17 cytokine (Buckley and Rast, 2017).
evidence: This is stated with a citation to Buckley and Rast, 2017.

claim: Echinochrome A is present in eggs of certain sea urchin species, in immune cells of the coelomic fluid of the adult (the red spherule cells), in spines, gonads, the digestive system, and in tube feet.
source: Echinochrome A is also present in eggs of certain sea urchin species, in immune cells of the coelomic fluid of the adult (the red spherule cells, RSC), in spines, gonads, the digestive system, and in tube feet (Brasseur et al., 2018; Coates et al., 2018; Johnson, 1969; Perry and Epel, 1981; Service and Wardlaw, 1984; Smith et al., 2018; Smith et al., 2010).
evidence: This is stated with multiple citations to previous work.

claim: The antimicrobial mechanism of echinochrome involves production of hydrogen peroxide and/or iron chelation.
source: The antimicrobial mechanism of echinochrome has not been completely resolved, but evidence suggests its production of hydrogen peroxide and/or iron chelation, abates microbial proliferation, (Coates et al., 2018; Lebedev et al., 2005; Perry and Epel, 1981).
evidence: This is stated with citations to previous work, though noted as not completely resolved.

claim: Sea urchin pigments have anti-microbial activity.
source: All of these studies agree that sea urchin pigments have anti-microbial activity, and that these small molecules may also contribute to states of cell physiology and gene expression (Jeong et al., 2014; Kim et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated with citations to previous studies.

claim: Pigment cells in the purple sea urchin originate from the non-skeletogenic mesoderm (NSM).
source: The developmental origins of pigment cells in the purple sea urchin have been traced to a group of mesodermal cells, the non-skeletogenic mesoderm (NSM) (Cameron et al., 1991; Croce and McClay, 2010; Materna and Davidson, 2012; McClay et al., 2000; Oliveri et al., 2002; Ruffins and Ettensohn, 1996; Sherwood and McClay, 1999; Sweet et al., 1999).
evidence: This is stated with multiple citations to previous work.

claim: Among the NSM cell types, pigment cells are specified first by Delta/Notch (D/N) signaling from the micromeres.
source: Among the NSM cell types, pigment cells are specified first by Delta/Notch (D/N) signaling from the micromeres (Calestani et al., 2003; Calestani and Rogers, 2010; Croce and McClay, 2010; Davidson et al., 2002a; Foster et al., 2020; Materna and Davidson, 2012; McClay et al., 2000; Oliveri et al., 2002; Ransick et al., 2002; Rast et al., 2002; Sherwood and McClay, 1999; Sweet et al., 2002; Sweet et al., 1999).
evidence: This is stated with multiple citations to previous work.

claim: Delta/Notch signaling directly activates the transcription factor glial cells missing (gcm).
source: The D/N signaling directly activates the transcription factor glial cells missing (gcm), which in turn activates several pigment cell genes, including: polyketide synthase1 (pks1), three flavin monooxygenases (fmo1, 2 and 3), a sulfotransferase (sult) and a dopachrome tautomerase (dopt) (Calestani et al., 2003; Calestani and Rogers, 2010; Davidson et al., 2002b; Ransick and Davidson, 2006; Ransick et al., 2002; Rast et al., 2002).
evidence: This is stated with citations to previous work.

claim: Gcm activates several pigment cell genes, including pks1, three flavin monooxygenases (fmo1, 2 and 3), a sulfotransferase (sult) and a dopachrome tautomerase (dopt).
source: The D/N signaling directly activates the transcription factor glial cells missing (gcm), which in turn activates several pigment cell genes, including: polyketide synthase1 (pks1), three flavin monooxygenases (fmo1, 2 and 3), a sulfotransferase (sult) and a dopachrome tautomerase (dopt) (Calestani et al., 2003; Calestani and Rogers, 2010; Davidson et al., 2002b; Ransick and Davidson, 2006; Ransick et al., 2002; Rast et al., 2002).
evidence: This is stated with citations to previous work.

claim: Pks1 and Fmo1 (reannotated as Fmo3) are required for the biosynthesis of echinochrome in pigment cells.
source: The enzymes Pks1 and Fmo1 (reannotated as Fmo3 in this study) are required for the biosynthesis of the echinochrome in pigment cells (Calestani et al., 2003).
evidence: This is stated with a citation to Calestani et al., 2003.

claim: Pks1 is required for any pigment biosynthesis in the adult.
source: Pks1 is required for any pigment biosynthesis in the adult while Fmo3 is required for accumulation of Spinochrome B in spines, but not for echinochrome synthesis in RSC and tube feet (Wessel et al., 2020).
evidence: This is stated with a citation to Wessel et al., 2020.

claim: Fmo3 is required for accumulation of Spinochrome B in spines, but not for echinochrome synthesis in RSC and tube feet.
source: Pks1 is required for any pigment biosynthesis in the adult while Fmo3 is required for accumulation of Spinochrome B in spines, but not for echinochrome synthesis in RSC and tube feet (Wessel et al., 2020).
evidence: This is stated with a citation to Wessel et al., 2020.

claim: Gcm and pks1 are first detected at blastula stage in a ring of NSM precursors surrounding the skeletogenic mesenchyme.
source: Genes expressed selectively in pigment cells, such as gcm and pks1, are first detected at blastula stage in a ring of NSM precursors surrounding the skeletogenic mesenchyme (SM) and later during blastula stage they become restricted to the aboral NSM (Calestani et al., 2003; Duboc et al., 2010; Gibson and Burke, 1987; Gustafson and Wolpert, 1967; Kominami et al., 2001; Materna et al., 2013; Ransick and Davidson, 2012; Ransick et al., 2002).
evidence: This is stated with multiple citations to previous work.

claim: During blastula stage, gcm and pks1 become restricted to the aboral NSM.
source: Genes expressed selectively in pigment cells, such as gcm and pks1, are first detected at blastula stage in a ring of NSM precursors surrounding the skeletogenic mesenchyme (SM) and later during blastula stage they become restricted to the aboral NSM (Calestani et al., 2003; Duboc et al., 2010; Gibson and Burke, 1987; Gustafson and Wolpert, 1967; Kominami et al., 2001; Materna et al., 2013; Ransick and Davidson, 2012; Ransick et al., 2002).
evidence: This is stated with multiple citations to previous work.

claim: At the gastrula stage, gcm and pigment biosynthetic genes are expressed in cells migrating into the blastocoel.
source: At the gastrula stage, gcm, as well as the pigment biosynthetic genes are expressed in cells migrating into the blastocoel, and their expression is maintained throughout larval development (Calestani et al., 2003; Gibson and Burke, 1987; Gustafson and Wolpert, 1967; Kominami et al., 2001; Ransick and Davidson, 2006; Ransick et al., 2002).
evidence: This is stated with citations to previous work.

claim: Expression of gcm and pigment biosynthetic genes is maintained throughout larval development.
source: At the gastrula stage, gcm, as well as the pigment biosynthetic genes are expressed in cells migrating into the blastocoel, and their expression is maintained throughout larval development (Calestani et al., 2003; Gibson and Burke, 1987; Gustafson and Wolpert, 1967; Kominami et al., 2001; Ransick and Davidson, 2006; Ransick et al., 2002).
evidence: This is stated with citations to previous work.

claim: In gcm knockdown embryos, pigment cells do not migrate to the ectoderm at the mesenchyme blastula stage, and pigments are lost.
source: Some evidence suggests gcm may be required for the development of pigment cells, since in gcm knockdown embryos, the cells do not migrate to the ectoderm at the mesenchyme blastula stage, and pigments are lost (Ransick and Davidson, 2006).
evidence: This is stated with a citation to Ransick and Davidson, 2006.

claim: Ectopic expression of gcm in skeletogenic mesoderm (SM) cells is sufficient to induce single cell migration to the ectoderm and accumulation of pigment in these cells, but not the acquisition of typical pigment cell morphology.
source: Moreover, ectopic expression of gcm in skeletogenic mesoderm (SM) cells is sufficient to induce a similar single cell migration to the ectoderm and the accumulation of pigment in these cells, but not the acquisition of the typical morphology of pigment cells (Damle and Davidson, 2012).
evidence: This is stated with a citation to Damle and Davidson, 2012.

claim: Gcm is expressed at higher levels in adult hematopoietic tissues, the pharynx and the axial organ, which produce new coelomocytes upon immune challenge.
source: Gcm is also expressed at higher levels in adult hematopoietic tissues, the pharynx and the axial organ, which produce new coelomocytes upon immune challenge (Golconda et al., 2019).
evidence: This is stated with a citation to Golconda et al., 2019.

claim: The ectodermal transcriptional state at single cell level reveals multiple cell-types, mostly of ectodermal origin.
source: The ectoderm-enriched single cell transcriptome revealed multiple cell-types, mostly of ectodermal origin as expected, and the overall cell cluster organization was highly reproducible between 48hpf and 72hpf samples (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by Figure 1B showing tSNE plots.

claim: The overall cell cluster organization was highly reproducible between 48hpf and 72hpf samples.
source: The ectoderm-enriched single cell transcriptome revealed multiple cell-types, mostly of ectodermal origin as expected, and the overall cell cluster organization was highly reproducible between 48hpf and 72hpf samples (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by Figure 1B.

claim: The pigment cell markers gcm and pks1 were found in clusters 2 and 13, which showed a similar transcriptome profile.
source: The pigment cell markers gcm and pks1 were found in clusters 2 and 13, which showed a similar transcriptome profile, and cluster 12, which had a transcriptomic profile that was distinct from clusters 2 and 13.
evidence: This is stated in the results describing the single cell analysis.

claim: Cluster 12 had a transcriptomic profile that was distinct from clusters 2 and 13.
source: The pigment cell markers gcm and pks1 were found in clusters 2 and 13, which showed a similar transcriptome profile, and cluster 12, which had a transcriptomic profile that was distinct from clusters 2 and 13.
evidence: This is stated in the results describing the single cell analysis.

claim: Cluster 12 expressed gcm, pks1, and the transcription factor six1 and its co-factor eya.
source: In addition to gcm and pks1, cluster 12 also expressed the transcription factor six1 and its co-factor eya, which are expressed in aboral secondary mesoderm at mesenchyme blastula (Poustka et al., 2007; Ransick and Davidson, 2012).
evidence: This is stated in the results with citations to previous work on six1 and eya expression.

claim: Six1 and eya are expressed in aboral secondary mesoderm at mesenchyme blastula.
source: In addition to gcm and pks1, cluster 12 also expressed the transcription factor six1 and its co-factor eya, which are expressed in aboral secondary mesoderm at mesenchyme blastula (Poustka et al., 2007; Ransick and Davidson, 2012).
evidence: This is stated with citations to Poustka et al., 2007 and Ransick and Davidson, 2012.

claim: Clusters 2 and 13 expressed gcm, pks1 and well-known pigment cell markers (fmo3, fmo5-1, sult1c2).
source: Cluster 2 and 13 expressed gcm, pks1 and well-known pigment cell markers (fmo3, fmo5-1, sult1c2 [Calestani et al., 2003; Ransick and Davidson, 2006; Ransick and Davidson, 2012; Ransick et al., 2002]).
evidence: This is stated in the results with citations to previous work identifying these markers.

claim: Gcm is dynamically expressed between many different cell states through development.
source: This analysis revealed 7 cell states of gcm-expressing cells, across the developmental time points (Figure 2A, Figure 2—figure supplement 1), showing that gcm is dynamically expressed between many different cell states through development.
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by Figure 2A showing integration across developmental stages.

claim: Gcm is transiently expressed in many different cell states.
source: This is an unusual feature for gene expression in that gcm is not just accumulating in more cell states as they appeared, but that gcm is transiently expressed in many different cell states.
evidence: This is stated as an interpretation of the single cell data showing dynamic gcm expression.

claim: Gcm may initiate various gene activities, but maintenance of that gene activity is dependent on other transcriptional mechanisms.
source: This suggests that gcm in this embryo may initiate various gene activities, but that maintenance of that gene activity is dependent on other transcriptional mechanisms.
evidence: This is stated as an interpretation of the transient expression pattern.

claim: Gcm was first detected at 64 cell stage, when there are nine gcm+ cells, 1% of total cells.
source: Using the dataset of Foster et al., 2020 we found that Gcm was first detected at 64 cell stage, when there are nine gcm+ cells, 1% of total cells.
evidence: This is stated in the Figure 2 legend based on analysis of the Foster et al., 2020 dataset.

claim: Pks1 was highly expressed in clusters 2 and 13, and at low levels in cluster 12 at gastrula stage.
source: Pks1 was highly expressed in cells of clusters 2 and 13, and at low levels in cells of clusters 12 at gastrula stage (see violin plot, Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by violin plots in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: The number of cells in cluster 2 increased from 48hpf to 72hpf, while the proportion of cells in cluster 13 decreased.
source: The number of cells in these two clusters changed from 48hpf to 72hpf. Over a period of 24 hours, the proportion of cells in cluster two increased, while the proportion of cells in cluster 13 decreased (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Cluster 13 expressed transcripts encoding S-phase and mitotic activities at high levels.
source: Both clusters expressed pigment cell markers at high levels, and the only difference was that cluster 13 (the cluster with fewer cells at both time points) also expressed transcripts encoding S-phase and mitotic activities at high levels.
evidence: This is stated in the results based on differential gene expression analysis.

claim: The elevated markers in cluster 13 included cdk1, pcna, DNA polymerases, DNA ligases, condensins, and centromere proteins.
source: The elevated markers in cluster 13 included cdk1, pcna, DNA polymerases, DNA ligases, condensins, and centromere proteins (Supplementary file 2), all genes that were absent in cluster 2.
evidence: This is stated in the results with reference to Supplementary file 2.

claim: From gastrula to early larva, cells that were in S-phase represented 34% of total pigment cells.
source: We found that from gastrula to early larva, cells that were in S-phase represented 34% of total pigment cells, and were broadly distributed in the embryos (Figure 2E,F,G).
evidence: This is stated in the results based on EdU pulse labeling experiments shown in Figure 2E,F,G.

claim: Mitotic pigment cells were broadly distributed in the embryos.
source: We found that from gastrula to early larva, cells that were in S-phase represented 34% of total pigment cells, and were broadly distributed in the embryos (Figure 2E,F,G).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 2E,F,G.

claim: Pigment cells have the ability to divide as migratory cells.
source: This finding of a mitotic pigment cell cluster suggests that pigment cells have the ability to divide as migratory cells.
evidence: This is stated as an interpretation of the EdU labeling and single cell data.

claim: In blastulae and gastrulae, pks1 and gcm were expressed in the same cells that have pigment cell morphology.
source: In blastulae and gastrulae, pks1 and gcm were expressed in the same cells that have pigment cell morphology (Figure 3A–B'').
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown by double FISH in Figure 3A–B''.

claim: In larvae, pks1 expression was maintained in pigment cells, while gcm expression transitioned into the left coelomic pouch.
source: In larvae, however, pks1 expression was maintained in pigment cells, while gcm expression transitioned into the left coelomic pouch, the site of the future adult rudiment (Figure 3C–C'').
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown by double FISH in Figure 3C–C''.

claim: ABCG11 is an ATP-binding cassette transporter homolog of the white half-transporter that transports pigment precursors and intermediates into the Drosophila eye.
source: Among these genes, ABCG11 is an ATP-binding cassette transporter homolog of the white half-transporter that transports pigment precursors and intermediates into the Drosophila eye (Mackenzie et al., 2000; Shipp and Hamdoun, 2012).
evidence: This is stated with citations to Mackenzie et al., 2000 and Shipp and Hamdoun, 2012.

claim: Abcg11 was selectively expressed in the pigment cell clusters 2 and 13, but not in cluster 12.
source: Abcg11 was selectively expressed in the pigment cell clusters 2 and 13, but not in cluster 12 (violin plots in Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by violin plots.

claim: Abcg11 was exclusively expressed in gcm and pks1 + cells.
source: Double FISH showed that Abcg11 was exclusively expressed in gcm and pks1 + cells (Figure 3D,E–E', F–F').
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown by double FISH in Figure 3.

claim: MIF (macrophage inhibitory factor) is a member of a gene family of cytokines that regulate innate immunity.
source: MIF (macrophage inhibitory factor) is a member of a gene family of cytokines that regulate innate immunity (Hibino et al., 2006; Nishihira, 2000).
evidence: This is stated with citations to Hibino et al., 2006 and Nishihira, 2000.

claim: Mif5 was expressed in the same gcm+ pigment cell clusters at 48hpf (2, 12, and 13), and by 72hpf it became enriched in the pigment cell clusters 2 and 13 exclusively.
source: Of these genes, mif5 was expressed in the same gcm+ pigment cell clusters at 48hpf (2, 12, and 13, violin plots in Figure 2—figure supplement 2), and by 72hpf it became enriched in the pigment cell clusters 2 and 13 exclusively.
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by violin plots.

claim: Oprk is a Cholecystokinin Receptor Type A, a G-protein coupled receptor that binds to cholecystokinin peptide hormones to modulate feeding and dopamine-induced behavior.
source: Opioid receptor, kappa 1-like (oprk) is a Cholecystokinin Receptor Type A, a G-protein coupled receptor that binds to cholecystokinin peptide hormones to modulate feeding and dopamine-induced behavior (Crawley, 1991).
evidence: This is stated with a citation to Crawley, 1991.

claim: Oprk was enriched in clusters 2, 12 and 13 at 48hpf, but by 72hpf it was enriched also in the ciliary band neurons (cluster 16).
source: scRNA-seq data showed that oprk was enriched in clusters 2, 12 and 13 at 48hpf, but by 72hpf it was enriched also in the ciliary band neurons (cluster 16), and we detected a spotty expression in this region by FISH (arrowhead in Figure 3L' and violin plots in Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by scRNA-seq data and FISH.

claim: GluR6 was not detectable by single cell sequencing at 48hpf.
source: GluR6 was not detectable by single cell sequencing at 48hpf, and double FISH analysis showed only faint signals in gcm+ cells (violin plots in Figure 2—figure supplement 2; Figure 3M–M').
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by violin plots and FISH.

claim: GluR6 was detectable at 72hpf at low levels in cluster 2 (differentiated pigment cells) and cluster 16, a cluster of neurons.
source: GluR6 was detectable at 72hpf though at low levels in cluster 2 (differentiated pigment cells) and cluster 16, a cluster of neurons.
evidence: This is stated in the results based on single cell data.

claim: GluR6 was highly expressed in both coelomic pouches.
source: GluR6 was also highly expressed in both coelomic pouches (Figure 3N–N' and inset), a tissue not included in the scRNA-seq enriched for the ectoderm.
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown by FISH in Figure 3N–N'.

claim: Genes for pigment cell function (besides gcm and pks1 in gastrulae) are never expressed in the mesodermal cluster (cluster 12), but rather in the mitotic (cluster 13) and post-mitotic (cluster 2) pigment cell clusters.
source: Altogether the single cell transcriptome data and double FISH on the transcripts found in the scRNA-seq dataset indicated that genes for pigment cell function (besides gcm and pks1 in gastrulae) are never expressed in the mesodermal cluster (cluster 12), but rather in the mitotic (cluster 13) and post-mitotic (cluster 2) pigment cell clusters.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the single cell and FISH data.

claim: Not all of the identified fmos were specifically expressed in pigmented cells.
source: To determine the expression of fmos in echinoderms, we sought all Fmo domains in the S. purpuratus genome (echinobase.org, V4.2; RRID:SCR_013732), and we found that not all of the identified fmos were specifically expressed in pigmented cells.
evidence: This is stated in the results based on phylogenetic and expression analysis.

claim: Phylogenetic analysis found 4 Fmo clades: one in the same clade with vertebrate Fmo proteins (clade 2), two not closely related to Fmo proteins in other organisms (clades 1 and 3), and one sub-family in the same clade with fly orthologs.
source: We performed a phylogenetic analysis to look for protein subfamilies, and found 4 Fmo clades: one is in the same clade with vertebrate Fmo proteins (clade 2), two are not closely related to Fmo proteins in other organisms (clades 1 and 3), and one sub-family is in the same clade with fly orthologs (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 4A phylogenetic tree.

claim: Only the fmo genes in clade one were found significantly enriched in both of the pigment cell states.
source: Among these 4 clades, only the fmo genes in clade one were found significantly enriched in both of the pigment cell states.
evidence: This is stated in the results based on single cell data analysis.

claim: Fmo5-1, fmo3 and fmo2-2 were all expressed in the mitotic and differentiated pigment cell clusters, but not in the mesodermal cluster 12.
source: Fmo5-1, fmo3 and fmo2-2 (previously named 1,2,3) were all expressed in the mitotic and differentiated pigment cell clusters, but not in the mesodermal cluster 12 (violin plots in Figure 4—figure supplement 1; Figure 4L–M).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by violin plots and heatmaps.

claim: Fmo5-1 and fmo3 were exclusively expressed in pigment cells.
source: We found that fmo5-1 and 3 were exclusively expressed in pigment cells, while fmo2-2 is expressed also in cells that are gcm-negative (Figure 4D–D').
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown by double FISH in Figure 4.

claim: Fmo2-2 is expressed also in cells that are gcm-negative.
source: We found that fmo5-1 and 3 were exclusively expressed in pigment cells, while fmo2-2 is expressed also in cells that are gcm-negative (Figure 4D–D').
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown by double FISH in Figure 4.

claim: Fmo2 was expressed at low level in a few cells of the blastocoel that are gcm/pks1 – and in tight apposition to the ectoderm.
source: In addition to the pigment cells, fmo2 was expressed at low level in a few cells of the blastocoel that are gcm/pks1 –. They are in tight apposition to the ectoderm (Figure 4E,E' and I,I').
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown by FISH in Figure 4.

claim: All fmos from clade one were enriched in pigment cells.
source: Overall, by scRNA-seq and FISH we found that all fmos from clade one were enriched in pigment cells.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the scRNA-seq and FISH data.

claim: In Hemicentrotus pulcherrimus, knocking out fmo3 resulted in a change in pigmentation of the adult, distinct from the albino phenotype of the pks1 gene knockout.
source: In a different sea urchin species (Hemicentrotus pulcherrimus), knocking out the gene function of fmo3 resulted in a change in pigmentation of the adult, distinct from the albino phenotype of the pks1 gene knockout (Wessel et al., 2020).
evidence: This is stated with a citation to Wessel et al., 2020.

claim: Only fmo2, located at the base of clade one in the phylogenetic tree, was not abundant in the embryo and had less than 250 transcripts/embryo.
source: Only fmo2, located at the base of clade one in the phylogenetic tree, was not abundant in the embryo and had less than 250 transcripts/embryo (Figure 5A,B).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 5A,B.

claim: Only clade one fmos are highly expressed in embryos.
source: Our experiments show that only clade one fmos are highly expressed in embryos (in agreement with our FISH and transcriptomic analyses), while the other clades of fmos are poorly or not detectable at all in embryos.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the transcript abundance and FISH data.

claim: At least one gene of clades 2, 3 and 4 was expressed in the spines, while fmos from clade one were lacking.
source: We found that at least one gene of clades 2, 3 and 4 was expressed in the spines, while fmos from clade one were lacking (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown by qPCR in Figure 5C.

claim: Coelomocytes expressed fmos from clade 1, but not the other fmos.
source: Coelomocytes, however, expressed fmos from clade 1, but not the other fmos (Figure 5E).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown by qPCR in Figure 5E.

claim: Pks1 was highly expressed in the adult immune cells, but expressed only at low levels in spines and tube feet.
source: We found that pks1 was highly expressed in the adult immune cells, but expressed only at low levels in spines and tube feet.
evidence: This is stated in the results based on qPCR data.

claim: Low levels of polyketide synthase gene activity are sufficient for maintenance levels of polyketide synthesis and pigmentation, especially in immune-quiescent animals.
source: We interpret these results as fmos might function independently from pks1, and that low levels of polyketide synthase gene activity are sufficient for maintenance levels of polyketide synthesis and pigmentation, especially in immune-quiescent animals (not challenged by bacteria).
evidence: This is stated as an interpretation of the qPCR results.

claim: Of the four fmo families, only clade 1 was found specifically in pigment cells of the embryo and in the adult red spherule cells, two cell-types with known immune functions.
source: Taken together, these results suggested that of the four fmo families, only clade 1 was found specifically in pigment cells of the embryo and in the adult red spherule cells, two cell-types with known immune functions.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the expression analysis across embryonic and adult tissues.

claim: Gastrulae in which gcm is knocked down have a unique phenotype with no pigmentation and low levels of pks1, sult1c2 and fmo3.
source: Gastrulae in which gcm is knocked down have a unique phenotype with no pigmentation and low levels of pks1, sult1c2 and fmo3 (Ransick and Davidson, 2006).
evidence: This is stated with a citation to Ransick and Davidson, 2006.

claim: In gcm morphants, the number of pigment cells decreases, and the expression of pigment gene markers is reduced.
source: ScRNA-seq of gcm morphants shows that in the absence of gcm the number of pigment cells decreases, and the expression of pigment gene markers is reduced.
evidence: This is stated in the results based on single cell analysis of gcm morphants.

claim: The pigment cell cluster population dramatically decreased by a factor of 7 with gcm knocked down by the morpholino.
source: While 40% of the clusters did not change size (Figure 6—figure supplement 1), the pigment cell cluster population dramatically decreased by a factor of 7 with gcm knocked down by the morpholino (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Gcm is responsible to specify pigment cells, and not just for driving expression of pigment cell genes.
source: We interpret this result as gcm is responsible to specify pigment cells, and not just for driving expression of pigment cell genes.
evidence: This is stated as an interpretation of the gcm morphant single cell data.

claim: The expression of gluR6 and fmo2, which were expressed in more cell-states than the pks1+ cells, was unchanged in gcm morphants.
source: The expression of gluR6 and fmo2, which were expressed in more cell-states than the pks1+ cells, was unchanged.
evidence: This is stated in the results based on qPCR of gcm morphants.

claim: Fmo2-2 from clade1, which was not detectable in the single cell experiment, was downregulated in the gcm morphant.
source: Fmo2-2 from clade1, which was not detectable in the single cell experiment, was downregulated in the gcm morphant.
evidence: This is stated in the results based on qPCR of gcm morphants.

claim: Genes like fmo2-3 and fmo5, not found in the pigment cell cluster, did not change expression in gcm morphant embryos.
source: Genes like fmo2-3 and fmo5, not found in the pigment cell cluster, did not change expression in gcm morphant embryos (Figure 6E).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 6E.

claim: Larvae of cas9-mediated knockout of pks1 were indistinguishable from control larvae when stained for Sp1 antibody.
source: In contrast, larvae of cas9-mediated knockout of pks1 were indistinguishable from control larvae when stained for Sp1 antibody (Figure 6F).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 6F.

claim: Not only the number, but also the distribution of pigment cells does not change in Pks1 depleted larvae.
source: Pigment cells stained with the Sp1 antibody show that not only the number, but also the distribution of pigment cells does not change in Pks1 depleted larvae.
evidence: This is stated in the results based on Sp1 staining of pks1 knockout larvae.

claim: Gene expression of candidate genes in pks1- larvae was also indistinguishable from controls.
source: Gene expression of candidate genes in pks1- larvae was also indistinguishable from controls (Figure 6—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 4.

claim: Pigmentation does not have a role in positioning pigment cells within the larvae, in regulating numbers or density of the pigment cells, or change overtly the physiology of the cells.
source: We conclude that pigmentation does not have a role in positioning these cells within the larvae, in regulating numbers or density of the pigment cells, or change overtly the physiology of the cells as this would have been revealed by the cellular phenotype or steady state levels of relevant candidate mRNAs.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the pks1 knockout experiments.

claim: There are fewer pigment cells in the gcm MO larvae compared to controls, and their localization appears to be randomly dispersed throughout the aboral ectoderm.
source: In agreement with the single cell data, we find fewer pigment cells in the gcm MO larvae compared to controls, and their localization appears to be randomly dispersed throughout the aboral ectoderm (Figure 6G).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 6G.

claim: Gcm knock down compromises the number of pigment cells.
source: Taken together our experiments show that gcm knock down compromises the number of pigment cells .
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the gcm morphant experiments.

claim: Gcm is not essential for all cell clusters expressing it, but has only a transient expression regulated at the transcriptional and/or post-transcriptional level.
source: Our conclusion is that gcm is not essential for all these clusters, but it has only a transient expression regulated at the transcriptional and/or post-transcriptional level.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the dynamic gcm expression analysis.

claim: Gcm may initiate transcription of certain genes, whose expression will be maintained by other regulatory factors following possibly an additional environmental cue or cell signaling.
source: This suggests either a housekeeping role for gcm that was underestimated, or a role in initiating transcription of certain genes, whose expression will be maintained by other regulatory factors following possibly an additional environmental cue or cell signaling.
evidence: This is stated as speculation about gcm function based on its transient expression pattern.

claim: Cluster 12 defines mesodermal pigment cell progenitors (six1 and eya markers), determined but not differentiated yet.
source: Last, of the three gcm+ clusters, cluster 12 defines mesodermal pigment cell progenitors (six1 and eya markers), determined but not differentiated yet.
evidence: This is stated as an interpretation of the cluster 12 gene expression profile.

claim: Gcm is responsible for specifying pigment cells, not just driving expression of pigment cell genes.
source: Here we show that gcm is responsible for specifying pigment cells, not just driving expression of pigment cell genes.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as a conclusion from the gcm morphant experiments.

claim: Despite gcm being necessary to specify most pigment cells, gcm-independent mechanisms appear to activate pigment cell identity when gcm activity is depleted.
source: Our results suggest that despite gcm being necessary to specify most pigment cells, gcm-independent mechanisms appear to activate pigment cell identity when gcm activity is depleted.
evidence: This is stated as an interpretation of the residual pigment cells in gcm morphants.

claim: All of the candidates identified in this study were enriched in the gcm+ transcriptome from a previous study.
source: To evaluate our single cell data in this comparative light, we searched for the pigment cell markers described in our study in the list of genes previously reported, and found that all of the candidates we identified were enriched in the above gcm+ transcriptome.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion comparing results to Barsi et al., 2015.

claim: Pigment cells expressing neuronal receptors suggests that they might also have a sensory function possibly coordinated with their immune response function.
source: The fact that pigment cells were expressing these neuronal receptors and others (this study and [Barsi et al., 2015]) suggests that they might also have a sensory function possibly coordinated with their immune response function.
evidence: This is stated as speculation based on the expression of neuronal receptors in pigment cells.

claim: The numbers of pigment cells expand if larvae are immune challenged.
source: What is clear is that the numbers of pigment cells expand if larvae are immune challenged (Kiselev et al., 2013; Ageenko et al., 2014; Wessel et al., 2020).
evidence: This is stated with citations to previous work.

claim: The transcript profile is distinct in the mitotic cohort and those cells are resistant to the gcm knockdown.
source: We favor the concept of a stem population for this lineage because the transcript profile is distinct in the mitotic cohort and those cells are resistant to the gcm knockdown.
evidence: This is stated as an interpretation of the mitotic cluster characteristics.

claim: Gcm is essential for the lineage expansion, but not for the stem precursors.
source: Perhaps Gcm is essential for the lineage expansion, but not for the stem precursors.
evidence: This is stated as speculation about gcm function in pigment cell development.

claim: Mitotic pigment cells do not seem to belong to a specific embryonic stem niche, but are distributed throughout the embryo.
source: These cells do not seem to belong to a specific embryonic stem niche, but are distributed throughout the embryo, suggesting that a portion of all pigment cells undergo mitosis to increase the pool.
evidence: This is stated based on EdU labeling showing distribution of mitotic pigment cells.

claim: Pigment cells from embryos of the sand dollar S. mirabilis and in the sea urchin S. intermedius can be induced to differentiate when cultured in the adult coelomic fluid in vitro.
source: Pigment cells from embryos of the sand dollar S. mirabilis and in the sea urchin S. intermedius can be induced to differentiate when cultured in the adult coelomic fluid in vitro, suggesting that genes involved in pigment synthesis in the adult also regulates pigment cells of the larva (Ageenko et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated with a citation to Ageenko et al., 2016.

claim: Adult coelomocytes from S. purpuratus express gcm, pks1 and group1 fmos.
source: Our finding that adult coelomocytes from S. purpuratus express gcm, pks1 and group1 fmos suggests that pigmented cells from the adult cells share biosynthetic and cell fate pathways.
evidence: This is stated based on qPCR data of adult coelomocytes.

claim: Pigmented cells from the adult cells share biosynthetic and cell fate pathways.
source: Our finding that adult coelomocytes from S. purpuratus express gcm, pks1 and group1 fmos suggests that pigmented cells from the adult cells share biosynthetic and cell fate pathways.
evidence: This is stated as an inference from the shared gene expression between embryonic and adult pigment cells.

claim: A population of pigment stem cells is set aside in the pre-metamorphosis larva to serve as a reservoir for the adult cells.
source: It has been suggested that in adult sea urchin a population of pigment stem cells is set aside in the pre-metamorphosis larva to serve as a reservoir for the adult cells (Wessel et al., 2020).
evidence: This is stated with a citation to Wessel et al., 2020.

claim: The embryonic mitotic cluster might be the cells that are selected in early embryos to replenish the larvae and/or adult stages.
source: We propose that the hereby-identified embryonic mitotic cluster might be the cells that are selected in early embryos to replenish the larvae and/or adult stages.
evidence: This is stated as a hypothesis about the function of the mitotic cluster.

claim: Pigmented cells in the diverse tissues of an adult are pigmented cells in distinct states.
source: However, as we learned here, pigmented cells in the diverse tissues of an adult are pigmented cells in distinct states.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the expression analysis of fmos in different adult tissues.

claim: The mitotic pigment cell cluster might represent a group of cells that retain the developmental potential that allows these cells to convert to other blastocoelar cells, or to the highly migratory pigment cells of the larvae.
source: An alternative hypothesis is that the pigment cell mitotic cluster serves in the embryo as a reservoir to replenish blastocoelar cell-types. We propose that the mitotic pigment cell cluster might represent a group of cells that retain the developmental potential that allows these cells to convert to other blastocoelar cells, or to the highly migratory pigment cells of the larvae.
evidence: This is stated as an alternative hypothesis about the function of the mitotic cluster.

claim: Cells with predicted similar functions (coelomic-pigmented cells versus larval-pigmented cells) have similar composition of pigment synthesizing enzymes and other gene expression.
source: In the case of cells with predicted similar functions, for example coelomic-pigmented cells (the red spherule cells), versus larval-pigmented cells, the composition of pigment synthesizing enzymes and other gene expression is instead similar.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion based on the qPCR data from adult and embryonic tissues.

claim: Cells with immune functions (adult coelomocytes and larval pigment cells) always express the same group of fmos, together with the enzyme pks1 and the transcriptional factor gcm.
source: Cells with immune functions (adult coelomocytes and larval pigment cells) always express the same group of fmos, together with the enzyme pks1 and the transcriptional factor gcm.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion based on the expression analysis.

claim: Both embryonic pigment cells and adult coelomocytes produce the pigment echinochrome A, a molecule with antimicrobial properties.
source: Both cells produce the pigment echinochrome A, a molecule with antimicrobial properties (Brasseur et al., 2018; Coates et al., 2018; Gerardi et al., 1990; Johnson, 1969; Lebedev et al., 2005; Perry and Epel, 1981), suggesting that gcm, pks1, and group1 fmos work together to make this unique pigment, but might not interact to make other echinoderm pigments.
evidence: This is stated with citations to previous work on echinochrome A.

claim: Gcm, pks1, and group1 fmos work together to make echinochrome A, but might not interact to make other echinoderm pigments.
source: Both cells produce the pigment echinochrome A, a molecule with antimicrobial properties (Brasseur et al., 2018; Coates et al., 2018; Gerardi et al., 1990; Johnson, 1969; Lebedev et al., 2005; Perry and Epel, 1981), suggesting that gcm, pks1, and group1 fmos work together to make this unique pigment, but might not interact to make other echinoderm pigments.
evidence: This is stated as an inference from the shared expression pattern in cells producing echinochrome A.

claim: Fmos are broadly expressed in yeast, plants and animals where their main role is detoxification.
source: Fmos are broadly expressed in yeast, plants and animals where their main role is detoxification (Dolphin et al., 1996; Janmohamed et al., 2001; Phillips et al., 1995; Phillips and Shephard, 2017).
evidence: This is stated with citations to previous work on Fmo function.

claim: Fmo enzymes catalyze the oxidation of different types of substrates that are involved in different types of biological processes across phyla: detoxification, metabolite activation, and in the case of the sea urchin, pigmentation.
source: Fmo enzymes catalyze the oxidation of different types of substrates that are involved in different types of biological processes across phyla: detoxification, metabolite activation, and in the case of the sea urchin, pigmentation and maybe more.
evidence: This is stated as general knowledge about Fmo function with specific application to sea urchins.

claim: Flies have two fmos, one with housekeeping functions and another involved in development.
source: Flies have two fmos, one with housekeeping functions and another involved in development (Scharf et al., 2004).
evidence: This is stated with a citation to Scharf et al., 2004.

claim: Human fmos are expressed in liver, lung, kidney and skin, cannot be induced or inhibited, and although being involved with drug metabolism, their physiological role is poorly understood.
source: Human fmos are expressed in liver, lung, kidney and skin (Peters, 1985; Schlaich, 2007), cannot be induced or inhibited, and although being involved with drug metabolism, their physiological role is poorly understood (Scharf et al., 2004).
evidence: This is stated with citations to previous work on human Fmos.

claim: Human Fmo3 is an enzyme that is constitutively active in the adult human liver where it participates in the oxidation of drugs and xenobiotics.
source: The most studied FMO is the human Fmo3, an enzyme that is constitutively active in the adult human liver where it participates in the oxidation of drugs and xenobiotics, and mutations in Fmo3 contribute to the disease trimethylaminuria (Cashman and Zhang, 2002; Dolphin et al., 1996; Krueger and Williams, 2005).
evidence: This is stated with citations to previous work on human Fmo3.

claim: Mutations in Fmo3 contribute to the disease trimethylaminuria.
source: The most studied FMO is the human Fmo3, an enzyme that is constitutively active in the adult human liver where it participates in the oxidation of drugs and xenobiotics, and mutations in Fmo3 contribute to the disease trimethylaminuria (Cashman and Zhang, 2002; Dolphin et al., 1996; Krueger and Williams, 2005).
evidence: This is stated with citations to previous work.

claim: Sea urchin spines are covered by a thin epithelium that is populated by pigmented cells marked with the embryonic pigment cell marker Sp1, most likely being red spherule cells.
source: Sea urchin spines are covered by a thin epithelium (Peters, 1985) that is populated by pigmented cells that we show here are marked with the embryonic pigment cell marker Sp1, most likely being red spherule cells.
evidence: This is stated based on Sp1 staining of spines shown in the results.

claim: The fmo clade two role might be connected to human Fmo function in the skin, where it might detoxify xenobiotics to which the spines are exposed in the seawater.
source: We suggest that the fmo clade two role might be connected to human Fmo function in the skin, where it might detoxify xenobiotics to which the spines are exposed in the seawater.
evidence: This is stated as speculation about the function of clade 2 fmos in spines.

claim: The sea urchin has at least 12 fmo genes that are not pseudogenes, since each are expressed at some time and place in the animal.
source: Only 1 fmo gene is present in yeast, whereas many flowering plants have 26 (Schlaich, 2007), two in flies (Scharf et al., 2004), six in humans (Dolphin et al., 1996) and at least 12 in sea urchin that are not pseudogenes, since each are expressed at some time and place in the animal.
evidence: This is stated based on the expression analysis showing all 12 fmos are expressed.

claim: The expansion of the fmo family in sea urchins might be necessary for the detoxification of a wide range of xenobiotics present in diverse ecosystems, especially benthic niches.
source: A hypothesis to explain this expansion is that such a variety of enzymes is necessary for the detoxification of a wide range of xenobiotics present in diverse ecosystems, especially benthic niches.
evidence: This is stated as a hypothesis to explain the fmo expansion.
